selection.note: Paris text for the earth entry (2026-11-17). Nollet's Leçons have no lesson on mineral bodies; Para (2 editions, 1772 and 1786) ties with Sigaud's Élémens (2), which do not treat them either, so Para is the next French course in the count that treats the topic. His third treatise, 'Théorie de la terre', takes in the earth's animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms. Also the Paris text for the terraqueous globe (2026-11-17): Nollet treats springs, the figure of the earth and volcanoes only inside lessons on water and gravity, under no heading of the globe, while Para's third treatise opens with a section of its own on the terrestrial globe (§§491-520); his fourth treatise, on water, supplies springs (§§667-679) and the saltness of the sea (§610).

selection.note: British text for motion, body, gravity and the system of the world from 2026-11-18, for water from 2026-11-20, for air and light from 2026-11-21, for the terraqueous globe from 2026-11-21, for electricity and the magnet from 2026-11-21, and for meteors from 2026-11-22, replacing the Britannica, which fails clause 2. Most-reprinted British course in the window (8 editions, against Nicholson 4, Rowning 3, Martin 3). Under clause 5 it is the British text for the topics it treats in a section of its own: matter, central forces (with headed passages on the laws of the planetary motions, Kepler's rule, the Cartesian vortices and 'the earth's motion demonstrated', which make him the text for the system of the world), the mechanical powers, hydrostatics, pneumatics and optics; the rest go to the next course in the count (Martin's Philosophical Grammar since 2026-11-21; Nicholson fails clause 12). Edition read: the 5th, London 1776, the one printed nearest 1775 with a public scan (the 1772 edition, IA b30501106, is the other candidate). Ferguson's text was also the Britannica's: see the note there. His separate Astronomy explained upon Sir Isaac Newton's Principles (1756; 1764 and later editions) is a single-topic treatise and fills no slot under clause 2; the Lectures send the reader to it for the astronomy proper (p. 26). The Britannica's Astronomy reprints it (see the note there). For water: Lecture V (hydrostatics, from p. 101) treats fluids in general and has nothing on water as a body (its qualities, purity, natural state, turning into earth) beyond a table of specific gravities (p. 159); the rise in narrow tubes is in Lecture I (p. 6), with no law of heights. For air (2026-11-21): Lecture VI, on pneumatics (pp. 168-178), and the air-pump experiments (pp. 179-200); the cause of the spring of air is in Lecture I (p. 8, the repulsive force of its particles); most of the air in bodies is 'fixed', released only by distillation, fermentation or putrefaction (p. 199, with Hales). For light: the lecture on optics, headed 'LECT. VIII.' on p. 201 (image), not VII as the contents worked out from the OCR had it; where Lecture VII begins was not checked. Light is particles flowing from the luminous body (p. 201), straight lines (p. 202), colours from different refrangibility (pp. 242-244); its velocity, 'at least a million times greater than the velocity of a cannon-ball', is in Lecture I (p. 5). For the terraqueous globe (2026-11-21, at Bruce's request, in place of the Nicholson proposed under R1 v4): no lecture on the globe, but headed passages on the tides (margin 'Of the tides', p. 41; running head p. 42, Lecture II), earthquakes (margin 'Earthquakes', p. 178, lecture on pneumatics), intermitting springs (margin, p. 117) and reciprocating springs and ebbing and flowing wells (Supplement, Hydrostatics, p. 20, its own heading); volcanoes close the earthquake passage without a heading (p. 179), and the figure of the earth follows the tides (pp. 46-47). His table of the moon's mean motion (p. 393, image) counts 'Years of the World' from 0 at 4008 before Christ, and Lecture XI calculates new and full moons 'from the creation of the world' (p. 377). The Lectures say nothing of fossil shells, strata, the origin of mountains, a central fire, the sea's saltness, the Flood or the theories of the earth (OCR of the whole book searched). The globe lectures are headed 'LECT. VIII. AND IX.' on p. 247 (image), so the number VIII is printed twice, for optics (p. 201) and for the globes. In the same lecture on pneumatics thunder and lightning come from fermenting sulphureous and nitrous effluvia (pp. 176-177, OCR), not from electricity; read for the meteors entry 2026-11-22 (see below). For electricity and the magnet (2026-11-21, images): Lecture I closes with two margin-headed passages, 'Magnetism' (pp. 17-18: the loadstone's three most remarkable properties, attracting iron and steel only, turning north and south, communicating its properties to steel; Helsham's inverse square at a balance, then 'some later experiments, made with the greatest accuracy', between the inverse square and the inverse cube) and 'Electricity' (pp. 18-19: amber, glass, jet, sealing-wax, agate and precious stones attract and repel light bodies when rubbed, 'electrical attraction', with seven observations on a rubbed glass tube; the effluvia snap against a finger). Magnetism and electricity are two of the four kinds of attraction (p. 6). Also: magnetism through the pores of gold (p. 15); knives struck by lightning magnetic for years, compasses reversed (p. 177); the variation of the compass found with the globe (p. 285). Thunder and lightning, under that margin heading (p. 176), are fermenting sulphureous and nitrous effluvia, not electricity. No Franklin, jar, machine, conductors, or positive and negative; Nollet only in the preface (leaf 9). Both passages are in the 1760 edition (OCR; 'late experiments' for 'later'). His separate Introduction to Electricity (1770; IA bim_eighteenth-century_an-introduction-to-elect_ferguson-james_1770), advertised on leaf 1 with sections on the machine, the protection of buildings from lightning and medical electricity, is a single-topic treatise (clause 2). These headed passages were overlooked when the globe was done ('every topic Ferguson treats is done'); the Lectures' margin headings were then checked for fire, the earth and meteors: fire and the earth went to Martin, meteors to Ferguson. Fire, checked 2026-11-21 (OCR of the whole book and the index; images of pp. 8, 15, 161): heat comes up only under the margin headings 'The expansion of metals' (p. 15, leading into the pyrometer) and 'The thermometer' (p. 161, with the expansion of fluids proportionable to the degree of heat); no passage on what fire or heat is, so fire goes to Martin. For meteors (2026-11-22, images of pp. 168, 173, 174, 176, 177, 189, 245-247): margin headings 'The cause of winds', 'The trade-winds' (p. 173), 'The monsoons' (p. 174), 'Fermentations', 'Thunder and lightning' (p. 176), 'Fire-damps' (p. 177); the rainbow without a heading at pp. 246-247 (index 'Rain-bow'); rain by the air growing too light to bear the vapours (p. 189). Thunder and lightning are fermenting sulphureous and nitrous effluvia; electricity is not invoked. The passages stand in the 1760 edition (OCR). His separate Introduction to Electricity (1770; IA bim_eighteenth-century_an-introduction-to-elect_ferguson-james_1770) describes Lind's apparatus for testing Franklin's lightning rods and treats lightning as electrical (OCR only); it is a single-topic treatise and fills no slot.

selection.note: Fails R1 clause 2 (encyclopedias do not qualify); supplementary since 2026-11-18. It was the British text of all thirteen pilot entries; the motion, body, gravity and system-of-the-world entries were redone with Ferguson on 2026-11-18, water on 2026-11-20, air, light, the terraqueous globe, electricity and the magnet on 2026-11-21, fire and the earth (with Martin) on 2026-11-21, and meteors (with Ferguson) on 2026-11-22, so no entry uses it as the British text any more. Its Pneumatics p. 490 (vol. 3 leaf 571, image) reprints Ferguson's thunder and lightning (Lectures 1776 pp. 176-177) and inserts '(see Electricity:)'; p. 493 (leaf 574) reprints his barometer before rain (p. 189). Its treatises Mechanics (vol. 3 from p. 32), Hydrostatics (vol. 2 from p. 804), and much of Pneumatics and Optics reproduce Ferguson's Lectures on Select Subjects nearly word for word (shared five-word sequences in the OCR, 2026-11-18: 25-40% of each page of Mechanics and Hydrostatics, 0% for control pages of Medicine and Money and for the Britannica's Astronomy, Electricity and Chemistry against the Lectures); short entries such as Inertia are its own. Its Mechanics leaves out Ferguson's examples of how far matter can be divided (Ferguson 1776 pp. 3-5: gold in silver, gold leaf, Leeuwenhoek's animalcules, the particles of light) and his sentence on the mountain (p. 3), all present in his editions of 1760 and 1770 (OCR, 2026-11-18). It follows an earlier edition than the fifth: after 'no weight or gravity of itself' (vol. 3 pp. 40-41) it has a sentence on Archimedes that the 1760 and 1770 editions have and the 1776 edition (p. 38) drops. Its Astronomy (vol. 1 from p. 434) is not its own either: it reprints Ferguson's separate Astronomy explained upon Sir Isaac Newton's Principles. Compared 2026-11-18 with the OCR of the 1764 edition (IA bim_eighteenth-century_astronomy-explained-upon_ferguson-james-f-r-s_1764; the 1770 scan's OCR is unusable): 32-71% of the five-word sequences on each page of vol. 1 pp. 434-449 (leaves 517-535) are Ferguson's, against 0% for control pages. The reprint is cut in places: in Ferguson's §§95-96 (pp. 28-29, read from the images) the Britannica's p. 445 (read from the image) drops 'everlasting' from Newton's 'everlasting foundation', 'and none who understand him can hesitate about it', and 'notwithstanding the opposition and violence of blind and zealous bigots' after Ptolemy's system was rejected. So Ferguson is the source of the Britannica's astronomy as of its mechanics; the Astronomy's tides (vol. 1 p. 473, leaf 568) are his too (49% of five-word sequences shared with his Astronomy, 1764 ed. p. 154; checked 2026-11-21). Its Mechanics also reprints the rest of Ferguson's Lecture II: the common centre of gravity and the regulating hand (vol. 3 pp. 41-42) and 'the earth's motion demonstrated' (pp. 42-43; vol. 3 leaf 54 = p. 41, 55 = p. 42, 58 = p. 43, from the images). For water (2026-11-20): its Chemistry 'Of Water' (vol. 2 pp. 66-67, leaves 85-86) and the entry Water (vol. 3 p. 936, leaf 847) are its own (0-1% of five-word sequences shared with the Lectures); its Hydrostatics (vol. 2 leaves 797-811, 25-37%) reprints Ferguson's Lecture V, and its text differs in small words from the 1776 edition ('so exceedingly small' for 'so small', 'since' for 'seeming', vol. 2 p. 804 against Ferguson p. 101, both read from the images), as an earlier edition would. For air (2026-11-21): its Pneumatics (vol. 3 from p. 484, leaf 565) reprints Ferguson's Lecture VI and his air-pump experiments up to no. 26 (leaves 565-566 and 571-575, 18-49%; beer and wood at p. 495, leaf 578), from an edition before the fifth: 17 grains for a quart of air, 14625 grains for a quart of water and 'three following particulars' (p. 484, read from the image), as in the 1760 and 1770 editions (OCR), against 16, 14621 and 'four' in 1776 (p. 169, p. 168, images). Its pp. 486-489 (leaves 567-570, 0-1%, on instruments) and its section 'Of winds' (leaf 579, 1%) are not Ferguson's. It leaves out Ferguson's miscellaneous experiments 27-32, his paragraph on fixed air and Hales's apples (Ferguson 1776 pp. 196-200; the fixed-air paragraph is also in the 1760 and 1770 editions, OCR). Its Mechanics (vol. 3 p. 34, leaf 45) reprints Ferguson's sentence on the repulsive force of the particles of air (p. 8). For light: its Optics from p. 416 (leaf 481) to the magic lantern (p. 427, leaf 492) reprints Ferguson's lecture on optics (19-45% per page); its section 'Different refrangibility of light' (from p. 427) and what follows (leaves 493-504, 0-2%) is not Ferguson's. Ferguson's velocity of light (p. 5) is in the passage its Mechanics leaves out. For the terraqueous globe (2026-11-21): the passages of its treatises cited there are Ferguson's, Mechanics p. 43 (leaf 58, 48%: the whirling-table tides and the figure of the earth, Lectures pp. 44-47), Pneumatics p. 491 (leaf 572, 35%: the earthquakes and volcanoes of Lectures pp. 178-179, reading 'set on fire' where the 1776 edition misprints 'set or fire') and Hydrostatics p. 808 (vol. 2 leaf 801, 52%: the intermitting springs of Lectures p. 117), and Astronomy p. 440 (leaf 523, 38%: the earth round like a globe, Ferguson's Astronomy p. 14). Its entries Terraqueous, Earth, Mountain, Sea, Earthquake, Vulcano, Deluge and Petrifaction are its own (0-1%); its Vulcano credits Lemery with the buried paste (fifty pounds, eight or nine hours) that Ferguson gives unattributed (10 or 15 pounds, 8 or 10 hours). The globe entry had cited the intermitting springs as Hydrostatics p. 847 (leaf 846); that leaf is p. 847, the entries Interest and Intermittent, and the passage is on p. 808 (image). For electricity and the magnet (2026-11-21): its treatise Electricity (vol. 2 leaves 412-428) is its own, sharing 0-1% of five-word sequences per page with Ferguson's Lectures (1776), his Introduction to Electricity (1770) and Martin's Philosophical Grammar (1762, 1769, 1778). Its Mechanics p. 36 (vol. 3 leaf 47, 45%, read from the image) reprints Ferguson's passage 'Magnetism' (Lectures pp. 17-18) word for word, with the first sentence of his 'Electricity', after which it sends the reader to the treatise; p. 35 (leaf 46) has his pores of gold (p. 15). Its entry Magnet (vol. 3 p. 3, leaf 14) is its own (0%). So in the magnet entry its claims on the three properties, the law of the force and 'iron and steel only' were Ferguson's; claims 003, 008, 012, 021 and 039 were corrected from these pages. For fire (2026-11-21): its entries Fire (vol. 2 leaves 548-550) and Heat (leaves 769-770) and its Chemistry 'Of Fire' (leaves 85-87) are its own, 0-1% of five-word sequences shared with Martin's Grammar (1762, 1769, 1778). For the earth (2026-11-21): its Chemistry (vol. 2 leaves 85-86, 96-98) and entry Alchemy (vol. 1 leaf 108) are its own, 0.1-0.5% of five-word sequences shared with Martin's Grammar (1762, 1778).

selection.source: Internet Archive holdings (ECCO scans), 2026-11-21: 1762, 1769, 1778. Lower bound; the ESTC was not consulted.
selection.note: First printed 1735, so clause 12 is met. Chosen 2026-11-21 (Bruce) as the British text for fire, the earth and meteors, after Nicholson (Introduction to Natural Philosophy, first edition 1782) failed clause 12; Rowning (A Compendious System of Natural Philosophy, 7th ed. 1772) has 3 editions too and is the second British text for meteors when that entry widens. Martin was also chosen that morning for electricity and the magnet, but the same day the reading of those entries showed that Ferguson's Lectures give both topics margin-headed passages (Lecture I pp. 17-19), which under the R1 v4 reading of clause 5 makes Ferguson (8 editions) their text; Bruce decided Ferguson for both, with Martin as the second British text when they widen. Before the Grammar is used for fire, the earth or meteors, check whether Ferguson has headed passages on them: he has 'Thunder and lightning' in the lecture on pneumatics (p. 176, image), which bears on meteors. Title-page problem: the 1778 printing calls itself the eighteenth edition and the 1769 the seventh; either the bookseller's numbering is inflated or the IA lacks many printings. An ESTC count by hand is needed; with more than 8 editions in the window the Grammar would outrank Ferguson for the topics both treat. Read for electricity and the magnet, 2026-11-21 (images): electricity is pp. 105-107, at the end of Part I ch. IX, 'Of Gravity and Levity: Of Attraction and Electricity' (from p. 94): electricity is 'a certain Kind of attractive Faculty, peculiar to some Bodies, as Amber, Jet, Sealing-Wax, Glass', whose particles, rarefied by the heat of rubbing, fly off and are drawn back by the body's attraction, 'as understood at present'; a note of sixteen properties of the rubbed tube (effluvia 'supposed to be of an unctuous and oily Nature') ends by sending the reader to Priestley's History. No Franklin, Nollet, jar, machine, conductors, or positive and negative (OCR of the whole book searched). Lightning is fermenting sulphureous and nitrous exhalations (p. 202). The note is already in the 1762 and 1769 printings (OCR); 1778 adds only the pointer to Priestley. The magnet: 'Wonderful Properties of the Loadstone', pp. 255-257, set apart from the catalogue of fossils in Part IV ch. II as 'this most wonderful of all Fossils': ten properties (no dip); the cause 'a Secret yet hid from Man, though he be blest with a Discovery of its Use' (p. 256); a note of authorities ending with Desaguliers, Whiston, Harris and Chambers (p. 257). Elsewhere: Halley's central magnet as the cause of the variation, 'very probable' (p. 238); iron 'of all Bodies… the only one attracted by the Loadstone' (p. 251); the electric fluid stopped by linen or paper while 'the magnetic Virtue pervades all Objects' (p. 106, note); Boerhaave via Shaw on the ashes of plants (p. 291, note). The book's index gives 'Magnet 225, 226, n.', a misprint for 255-256. Compared by shared five-word sequences, the Britannica's Electricity (vol. 2 leaves 412-428), its entry Magnet (vol. 3 leaf 14) and its Mechanics pp. 32-36 (leaves 43-47) share nothing with the Grammar (0-1% per page against the 1778, 1769 and 1762 OCR); the 1769 and 1762 texts of the same pages share 33-81% with 1778. Fire (2026-11-21): Ferguson's margin headings touch heat only under 'The expansion of metals' (p. 15) and 'The thermometer' (p. 161), and he gives fire and heat no passage of their own, so the Grammar is the British text for fire. Read from the images: the elements, p. 35; rarefaction, p. 111; fluidity, p. 113; 'Of Heat, Cold, &c.', pp. 114-116 (heat 'in the hot Body, Activity or Motion, and nothing else'; flame a fluid in motion that needs air; 'the Particles of Light and Fire are the same'); the note on vapours, p. 197 ('That Heat is Fire, and that the Particles of Fire are in a constant and violent Agitation'), which contradicts p. 114. The passage on heat is already in the 1762 printing (OCR). The Britannica's Fire, Heat and Chemistry 'Of Fire' (vol. 2 leaves 548-550, 769-770, 85-87) share 0-1% with the Grammar (1762, 1769, 1778). Read for the earth, 2026-11-21 (images of pp. 236, 239-242, 245-248, 251-253, 255 note, 257; OCR of pp. 249-250): Part IV ch. II, pp. 236-258, seven heads of earthy bodies (earths, ores, fossils = salts and sulphurs, minerals, metals, stones, extraneous bodies); metals of mercury and sulphur, the 'Sulphur of Metal' supposed the matter of light or fire (pp. 251-252); quicksilver 'incapable of congealing or freezing' (p. 248); minerals, metals and stones grow 'Undoubtedly', mines recruit, seeds of metals from the Creator, mountains as matrices (pp. 240, 257); no phlogiston, platina, transmutation or reduction of calces (OCR of the whole book). The chapter, these passages included, already stands in the 1762 printing (OCR). The Britannica's Chemistry (vol. 2 leaves 85-86, 96-98) and Alchemy (vol. 1 leaf 108) share 0.1-0.5% of five-word sequences with Martin 1762 and 1778. 2026-11-22: meteors went to Ferguson, not Martin, by the same reading (margin headings on the winds, pp. 173-174, and on thunder and lightning, p. 176); Martin and Rowning are the British texts to add when the meteors entry widens. The Grammar is the British text for fire and the earth only.
